articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document, titled 'EPHEMERIS Vol. 2 No. 4', is the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association for April 1990. It serves as a historical record of the club's activities and information for that specific month.

articles.title: FIELD OF VIEW
articles.summary: The article announces several April events for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), including a technical presentation by Kevin Medlock on his electronic CCD imaging camera and the 48-inch Schmidt camera project. It details multiple public star parties at Branham Lane Park, Henry Coe Park, Grant Ranch, and Glacier Point, with specific instructions for sign-ups and free camping availability. The annual Astronomy Day celebration at Branham Lane Park is also highlighted, featuring both afternoon solar observing and evening sessions.

articles.title: YOSEMITE STAR PARTY
articles.summary: The annual SJAA/Yosemite star party is scheduled for the weekend of July 20th and 21st. This event is planned to coincide with a moonless period, indicating optimal conditions for astronomical observation.

articles.title: ASTRONOMICAL AUCTION
articles.summary: The 10th Annual Astronomical Auction is scheduled for May 5th at the Red Cross building in Los Gatos, featuring both an afternoon flea market/swap meet (2-5 PM) and a main auction (starting 6 PM). Attendees can also participate in silent-bid sales, with specific guidelines for item placement between the flea market and auction. SJAA collects a 10% sales commission, and a $1 registration fee is requested for buyers and sellers, with pre-registration strongly encouraged.

articles.title: ASTRONOMY DAY
articles.summary: National Astronomy Day is scheduled for April 28, with the goal of promoting astronomy and telescope making. The Astronomical Association of Northern California will host an event at Branham Lane Park, while the Fremont Peak Observatory Association will feature John Briggs and their 30-inch reflector telescope as part of their program that evening.

articles.title: HUMAN SKELETON FOUND ON MOON
articles.summary: The provided document consists solely of a satirical headline, "HUMAN SKELETON FOUND ON MOON," which is explicitly identified as a humorous or fictional element. There is no actual article content to analyze beyond this title.

articles.title: BRANHAM LANE STAR PARTIES WE WANT YOU!
articles.summary: The SJAA is organizing a series of public star parties on various Fridays from April to December, inviting participants to bring telescopes and share the event with friends. Specific dates are provided, and contact information for Tom Ahl or Jim Van Nuland is mentioned for further details.

articles.title: MARCH STARRY NIGHTS
articles.summary: The article, titled "MARCH STARRY NIGHTS," begins with a whimsical, first-person narrative detailing the author's encounter with a small, green, red-haired individual after the effects of the Blarney Stone fade. The provided content is an incomplete, fantastical story opening and does not contain any astronomical or observing information.

articles.title: APRIL 7TH GENERAL MEETING KEVIN MEDLOCK CCD CAMERA TECHNIQUES
articles.summary: This document outlines upcoming astronomical events for April and early May, including several public star parties, SJAA board meetings, and an introductory observational astronomy class. A key event is the April 7th General Meeting, which will feature Kevin Medlock presenting on CCD camera techniques.

articles.title: THE CELESTIAL TOURIST SPEAKS
articles.summary: Jay Reynolds Freeman advocates for the utility of low-powered, unmounted telescopes, specifically a 4-6 inch f/5 Newtonian reflector, as an excellent intermediate instrument for amateur astronomers. He shares his positive personal experiences with a 6-inch f/5 reflector he built, emphasizing its portability, quick setup, and effectiveness for deep-sky observation using a hand-braced technique without a formal mount. Freeman recommends such instruments for budget-conscious observers beyond the raw beginner stage who are interested in deep-sky objects.

articles.title: PART THREE - CATADIOPTRIC CATATONIA, OR HOW I LEARNED HOW TO STOP COLLIMATING AND LOOK A THE SKY
articles.summary: The author chronicles their intense struggle with achieving perfect collimation for catadioptric telescopes, particularly a challenging Schmidt-Cassegrain (SCT). They describe overcoming initial failures and the flawed use of internal collimators, eventually realizing that proper SCT alignment requires using an artificial or real star at the exact magnification intended for observing. This crucial insight, accounting for primary mirror shift during focusing, finally allowed them to achieve optimal performance and reclaim their enjoyment of the night sky.

articles.title: THE NORTHERN SOUTHERN CROSS
articles.summary: While doing fieldwork in Phoenix, Arizona, Patrick M. Donnelly observed an asterism within the constellation Gemini that strongly resembled the Southern Cross, which he named the "Northern Southern Cross." Composed of stars like Pollux, Kappa Gemini, Iota Gemini, and Delta Gemini, this asterism mirrored the proportions of the actual Southern Cross despite being larger and dimmer. Donnelly details specific star correspondences, such as Pollux aligning with Gamma Crucis.

articles.title: GREAT RED SPOT
articles.summary: An observing report from a star party at Henry Coe State Park describes an unexpectedly excellent viewing experience on February 24, with 10/10 seeing despite haze and clouds. Observers clearly viewed Jupiter's Great Red Spot, which appeared notably red for the first time since 1976, along with other planetary features, emphasizing the importance of good seeing and moderate magnification for such observations.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article discusses Comet Austin, noting it is a new comet to the inner solar system that exhibited early brightness due to volatile chemicals. Despite not being bright enough to cast shadows, it is expected to put on a good show, especially during its close passage to Earth (22 million miles) in May, though it will appear large and require dark skies. The author provides ephemeris details and notes its proximity to M33 on April 12 and M31 on April 24.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: ASTRO ADS is a free classifieds section for non-commercial advertisers to sell astronomically related products or services. Ads are submitted to the editor by the 15th of each month and run for approximately three months. The section features examples of various used astronomy equipment for sale or trade, such as lenses, mirror kits, and refractors.

articles.title: CONSUMER SCIENTIFIC
articles.summary: CONSUMER SCIENTIFIC is a retailer specializing in science and nature products for hobbyists and professionals. They offer a diverse range of items including optics, books, science kits, labware, chemicals, maps, globes, and weather instruments, and are located in Mountain View, CA.

articles.title: SIAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document, titled 'SIAA EPHEMERIS,' serves as a classifieds section for astronomical equipment. It lists various used telescopes, optical components such as achromats, mirrors, and prisms, along with accessories like eyepieces, finders, and filters, all available for sale. Contact information and prices are provided for each listing, indicating a marketplace for amateur astronomers.

articles.title: OFFICERS AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors for an organization. It details their specific roles, such as President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, Editor, and Director, along with their names and contact phone numbers.

articles.title: COMET EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for two comets, Comet Austin (1989c₁) and Comet Skorichenko-George (1989e₁), detailing their predicted positions and brightness from late March through early May. For each comet, it lists daily or multi-daily data including Right Ascension (RA), Declination (DEC) for both 1950 and 2000 epochs, solar elongation, visibility in the sky, and apparent magnitude, aiding observers in locating and tracking these celestial objects.

articles.title: JUPITER'S RED SPOT
articles.summary: This document provides a viewing schedule for Jupiter's Great Red Spot (GRS). It lists specific dates and times in Pacific Standard Time (PST) during April and early May when the GRS will be transiting the meridian, indicating optimal visibility for observation. This serves as a guide for astronomers and enthusiasts to plan their viewing sessions.

articles.title: SPOT-2 EARTH RESOURCES SPACE-CRAFT LAUNCHED
articles.summary: The French SPOT-2 Earth Resources Space-craft was successfully launched on January 21 aboard a European Ariane-4 booster. The satellite has commenced transmitting high-resolution panchromatic and multispectral images.

articles.title: FUNDS FOR RETURNING TO THE MOON AND GOING TO MARS
articles.summary: A proposed budget of $15.1 billion includes significant funds for returning to the Moon by 2010 and aiming for Mars by the mid-21st century, with $216 million specifically allocated for lunar base/Mars technology. The budget also details allocations for various other space projects, including a Lunar Observer spacecraft, Earth observation platforms, Lifesat, Space Station Freedom, space shuttle operations, and the Advanced X-ray Astrophysics Facility (AXAF).

articles.title: VOYAGER 1 SNAPS SOLAR SYSTEM FAMILY PHOTO
articles.summary: Voyager 1 utilized its wide-angle camera in February to capture a mosaic image of the solar system's planets. This event is described as snapping a "solar system family photo."

articles.title: GALILEO MAKES VENUS FLYBY
articles.summary: The Galileo spacecraft successfully completed its closest approach to Venus on February 9th, gaining 4990 mph for its journey to Jupiter. It recorded 81 images and other data, most of which will be played back in October. This flyby also improved fuel margins, making a subsequent flyby of the asteroid Ida more probable.

articles.title: CONSTRUCTION OF ENDEAVOUR IS PROCEEDING
articles.summary: Construction of the Space Shuttle Endeavour is actively proceeding, with major components like the fuselage and flight crew compartment now at the Palmdale assembly plant. The construction has greatly benefited from a structural spares program initiated by NASA before the Challenger accident. Looking ahead, NASA is requesting $52 million for structural spares in FY 1991 to ensure readiness for potential future orbiter damage or loss.

articles.title: SOVIETS FLY MANNED MANEUVERING UNIT
articles.summary: Soviet cosmonauts conducted multiple EVAs using a Manned Maneuvering Unit (MMU) in early February. Following these activities, a new crew docked with the Mir space station on February 13th, replacing the previous crew who returned to Earth after six months. The new crew's mission includes processing materials in the upcoming Kristal Technological Module, which is also designed to support docking with the Soviet space shuttle Buran.

articles.title: PACIFIC TDRS PROBLEM
articles.summary: A TDRS satellite in the Pacific region has an antenna stuck in left circular polarization mode, limiting its ability to track multiple spacecraft for data relay. This issue could impact critical missions like Landsats 5 and 6 and the Hubble Space Telescope, which require right circular polarized transmissions. NASA is exploring solutions including modifying shuttle Ku-band systems, reactivating an orbital TDRS spare, and planning a new TDRS launch in January 1991.

articles.title: PREPARING FOR COMET AUSTIN
articles.summary: This article offers practical astrophotography advice for observers preparing to photograph Comet Austin, expected in late April and May. Drawing on lessons from Comet Halley, it emphasizes using fast lenses (f/4 or faster), high ISO film, and minus-violet filters for successful early morning captures. The guide also covers exposure bracketing, guiding techniques for different focal lengths, and essential equipment considerations to achieve sharp, well-composed images.

articles.title: The tenth annual Bay Area Astronomical Auction
articles.summary: The article announces the tenth annual Bay Area Astronomical Auction, detailing the process for sellers to pre-register their astronomical or telescope-making related items. It outlines instructions for submitting items, setting minimum bids, and specifies a 10% commission or outright donation benefiting public education in astronomy. Additionally, the event will feature a Swap Meet for smaller items and a Silent Bid option for large-ticket items like complete telescopes.

articles.title: DIRECTIONS to the Red Cross building
articles.summary: This document provides detailed directions to the Red Cross building for an event featuring a swap meet from 2-5 pm and an auction starting at 6 pm, with a requested $1 donation for registration. It also includes a registration form for the '1990 SJAA Auction' to list items for sale. Attendees are encouraged to car-pool and refreshments will be available.
